summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a man with chronic systolic heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and a history of heavy alcohol use, was admitted after being found down intoxicated with complaints of left-sided chest pain. Initial evaluation ruled out acute cardiac event, pulmonary embolism, or aortic dissection via normal troponins, EKG, and CT imaging. The chest pain was determined to be musculoskeletal, reproducible on palpation and exacerbated by movement. He exhibited signs of alcohol withdrawal, managed with diazepam per CIWA protocol. His heart failure and hypertension were stable, with no decompensation; home medications including metoprolol, losartan, and furosemide were continued. He admitted non-compliance with Dabigatran, and was counseled on the importance of anticoagulation due to prior pulmonary embolism. He improved clinically, remained alert and coherent, and was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to monitor weight, continue all medications, and follow up with his primary care provider.
